abstract: Despite the promise of ferroptosis in cancer therapy, its insufficient potency and off-target toxicity remain significant challenges. Few studies have explored the therapeutic potential of nanoparticle (NP)-mediated active targeting strategies to induce robust ferroptosis in colon cancer (COC) cells effectively. In this study, we developed sialic acid (SA)-targeted NPs by conjugating artesunate (ART) with alanine (Ala) and phenylboronic acid (PBA) to formulate ART-Ala-PBA NPs (AAP NPs). Compared with nontargeted ART-Ala NPs, AAP NPs accumulated significantly within cancer tissues, inhibited tumor growth, and improved the survival rates of mice with COC, while exhibiting minimal toxicity. Mechanistically, AAP NPs induce ferroptosis through the accumulation of reactive oxygen species and the downregulation of the SLC7A11-GPX4 axis. Deep data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics revealed a novel suppression of ribonucleotide reductase regulatory subunit M1 (RRM1), which synergizes with canonical ferroptosis pathways to amplify lipid peroxidation. RNA sequencing further indicated that AAP NPs uniquely modulate autophagy-related processes, suggesting a multimodal mechanism distinct from the alterations in amino acid metabolism induced by parental ART formulations. Collectively, AAP NPs represent the first carrier-free nanoassembly leveraging PBA-mediated SA targeting to co-activate ferroptosis via dual ROS/GPX4-RRM1 regulation, offering a translatable paradigm for precision nanotherapy of COC. Introduction
Colon cancer (COC) is a common and incurable malignant tumor that has become a remarkable global public health issue [
1
]. The currently available treatments cannot significantly increase the five-year survival rate of COC patients because of metastasis and resistance to chemotherapy [
2
]. The optimization of treatment regimens, such as rationally designed combination therapies, has made progress in overcoming chemotherapy resistance [
3
–
6
]. Currently, only a tiny population of COC patients with deficient mismatch repair (dMMR) benefit from immune checkpoint blockade (ICB)-based immunotherapy despite its success in immunogenically “hot” tumors [
7
–
9
]. Therefore, identifying new targets to increase the efficacy of chemotherapy and immunotherapy is a promising approach for achieving durable responses [
10
–
12
].
Ferroptosis, a distinct form of cell death that differs from apoptosis and necrosis, relies on iron and involves the accumulation of toxic lipid peroxides [
13
–
15
]. Increasing evidence has demonstrated that activating the ferroptosis-executing system and inhibiting the ferroptosis defensive system of cancer cells is a practical approach for treating COC [
16
–
20
]. Mechanistically, activating the ferroptosis-executing system mainly enhances the Fenton reaction, which can be amplified by increasing the amount of intracellular iron and H
2
O
2
[
21
–
24
]. However, increasing Fe
2+
levels through external sources such as iron-based nanomaterials is associated with health risks due to excess metals [
25
]. Additionally, the canonical ferroptosis defense mechanism is predominantly mediated by the GPX4/SLC7A11 signaling pathway [
26
,
27
] by assisting in intracellular glutathione (GSH) synthesis and alleviating LPO [
28
,
29
].
Artesunate (ART) is an FDA-approved, effective antimalarial drug with promising effects on various malignancies [
30
]. ART may inhibit the expression of SLC7A11, hinder the biosynthesis of GSH, downregulate GPX4, and ultimately disrupt the biofilm structure [
31
]. However, its poor water solubility and nonspecific biodistribution attenuate its therapeutic effect. Moreover, the antineoplastic activity of ART is weak when it is used as monotherapy. In contrast, high doses may result in side effects such as embryotoxicity, neurotoxicity, and immunotoxicity, severely limiting their clinical application [
32
,
33
].
To overcome these limitations, we developed a rational design strategy: modifying ART with biocompatible alanine (Ala) to enhance solubility and biological activity [
34
,
35
], followed by conjugation with phenylboronic acid (PBA) for active targeting [
36
,
37
]. PBA selectively binds to sialic acid (SA)-overexpressing glycans on COC cells, a hallmark of tumor invasiveness and drug resistance [
38
]. The resulting derivative (AAP) was formulated into nanomedicines further to enhance bioactivity and solubility [
39
–
41
]. Critically, unlike conventional ligand-modified nanocarriers, AAP NPs self-assemble into carrier-free nanostructures, eliminating excipient-related toxicity and maximizing drug loading efficiency. Given the above characteristics, natural amino acids and PBA were selected to modify the ART structure, aiming to improve its physicochemical properties and increase its antitumor activity.
Herein, we report a SA-targeted nanoassembly (AAP NPs) that co-opts both canonical (ROS/SLC7A11-GPX4) and novel (RRM1-suppressive) ferroptosis pathways (Scheme
1
). Through integrated proteomics/transcriptomics, we further unveil autophagy modulation as a complementary mechanism, positioning AAP NPs as a multimodal ferroptosis inducer with superior specificity and efficacy against COC. These promising findings offer a paradigm shift in actively targeted ferroptosis therapies and present AAP NPs as a potential for clinical translation in COC treatment.

Materials and methods
Materials
Unless mentioned otherwise, all chemicals and solvents were obtained from Titan Scientific, Aladdin, and Bidepharm in Shanghai, China. The structures of the compounds were identified via NMR spectroscopy (¹H and ¹³C NMR, with TMS as the internal standard, on a Bruker Avance III 400 spectrometer, Germany) and mass spectrometry (Waters ACQUITY QDa mass detector, Waters, Milford, Massachusetts, USA). The analysis of compound purity was conducted via high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, 1290 Infinity II, Agilent, Waldbronn, Germany) on a Hypersil ODS-C18 column (4.6 mm × 200 mm, 5 μm; mobile phase: water/methanol; flow rate: 1 mL/min; detection wavelength: 230 nm). The UV-visible absorption spectrum was captured via a UV-3600 UV-vis-NIR spectrometer (Shimadzu, Tokyo, Japan).
Cell culture
The CT26, HuH7, SW480, SW620, HIEC6, and NIH/3T3 cell lines were obtained from the Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and were maintained in RPMI 1640 medium (GBICO, CA, USA), Leibovitz’s L-15 medium (GBICO, CA, USA) or DMEM (GBICO, CA, USA) at 37 °C with 5% CO
2
, respectively. The HCT116 cell line was purchased from Shanghai Jinyuan Biotechnology Co., Ltd. and was cultured in McCoy’s 5 A medium (GBICO, CA, USA). All cell culture media contained 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; PAN-Biotech, Germany) and 50.0 IU/mL streptomycin and penicillin (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA).
Synthesis of ART-amine acid derivatives
A mixture of artesunate (0.5 g, 1.30 mmol, 1 eq),
L
-amino acid (1.43 mmol, 1.1 eq), HATU (0.74 g, 1.95 mmol, 1.5 eq), Et
3
N (0.26 g, 2.60 mmol, 2 eq), and tetrahydrofuran (10 mL) was stirred at 40 °C for 10–12 h. Tetrahydrofuran was evaporated under reduced pressure, and the residue was dissolved in dichloromethane (DCM, 20 mL). The solution was then washed with 10% aqueous citric acid (20 mL) and brine (20 mL), dried over anhydrous magnesium sulfate (MgSO
4
), and filtered. The solvent was then evaporated, and the residue was purified via flash column chromatography (CH
2
Cl
2
/MeOH/HAc) to obtain the ART-amine acid compounds. (The NMR data and spectra are shown in the Supporting Information.)
Synthesis of ART-amine acid-PBA derivatives
A solution of EDCI (0.13 g, 0.66 mmol, 1.5 eq) in DCM (10 mL) was added dropwise to ART-Ala (0.2 g, 0.44 mmol, 1 eq), aminophenylboronic acid (0.48 mmol, 1.1 eq), and HOBt (0.07 g, 0.53 mmol, 1.2 eq) in DCM (10 mL) at 0 °C. The mixture was stirred at 40 °C for 6–10 h and then washed with 10% aqueous citric acid (20 mL) and brine (20 mL). The mixture was dried over anhydrous magnesium sulfate (MgSO
4
), filtered, and then the solvent was evaporated. The residue was purified via flash column chromatography (CH₂Cl₂/MeOH/HAc) to yield the AAO, AAP, and AAQ target compounds. Compound AAR was synthesized from ART-Ala and 3-hydroxyphenyl boronic acid (3-hydroxy-PBA) in the presence of DMAP and EDCI. The AAS compound was synthesized from ART and 3-hydroxy-PBA via synthesis procedures similar to those used for AAO-AAQ. (The NMR data and spectra are shown in the Supporting Information.)
In vitro Sialic acid expression assay
The cells (tumor cells: CT26, HCT116, HuH7, SW620 and SW480 cells; normal cells: murine fibroblast cell line NIH/3T3 and human intestinal epithelial cells (HIEC6 cells) were lysed on ice in RIPA buffer (Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, Missouri, USA) at 12000 rpm at 4 °C for 10 min, and the protein concentration was determined via the BCA method (Elabscience, Wuhan, Hubei, China). Subsequently, equivalent protein amounts were loaded onto 10% SDS-PAGE gels and resolved. The protein was transferred to PVDF membranes, and the membranes were blocked in 5% non-fat dry milk in PBS, and incubated with primary antibodies at 4 °C overnight (Anti-Neu5Ac/O-sialic acid/Polysialic acid Antibody: 1:1000, AntibodySystem, San Diego, California, USA; GAPDH: 1:50000, Proteintech, Wuhan, Hubei, China). The sections were subsequently incubated with secondary antibodies (Goat anti-mouse IgG-HRP or goat anti-rabbit IgG-HRP, Proteintech, Wuhan, Hubei, China). The immunoblots were visualized via a chemiluminescence imaging system (Tanon-5200Multi, Shanghai, China) with enhanced chemiluminescence detection reagents.
Preparation and characterization of ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, and AAP NPs
NPs were formulated through the nanoprecipitation process. Specifically, 1 mL of an acetone solution (1 mg/mL) containing ART, ART-Ala, or AAP was added incrementally to 8 mL of distilled water under continuous stirring at 2000 rpm, facilitating the self-assembly of the NPs. The acetone was subsequently removed through evaporation, and the resulting residue underwent ultrafiltration and centrifugation to isolate the NPs. A Malvern Zetasizer (Nano-ZS90, Malvern, UK) was used to measure the hydrated particle size, distribution, and zeta potential at 25 °C. The morphological properties of the ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, and AAP NPs were observed via transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-1200EX, Tokyo, Japan) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Regulus8100, Tokyo, Japan). The physiological stabilities of ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, and AAP NPs were evaluated by recording their hydrated diameters upon incubation in distilled water, PBS, and 10% FBS-containing solution (pH 7.4) (1:20, v/v) for various time intervals.
Drug release in vitro
The drug release patterns of ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, and AAP NPs were assessed in vitro via buffer solutions at pH values of 5.5, 6.5, and 7.4. Briefly, ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, and AAP NPs were dispersed in 2 mL of buffer solution in a dialysis bag. A total of 200 µL of solution was collected at a given time, and then the exact amount and the same pH value of the buffer solution were replenished. The drug content of the collected solutions was measured via high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) at 230 nm.
In vitro cytotoxicity assay
The tumor cells (5 × 10
3
) were seeded in 96-well plates, incubated overnight, and then exposed to various compounds or NPs for 48 h. Afterward, the cells were washed with PBS. CCK8 solution (10 µL, Enogene, Shanghai, China) was added to each well and incubated for 2 h. The absorbance of each well was measured at 450 nm.
Cellular uptake of ART-Ala NPs and AAP NPs
Coumarin-6 (Cou-6) was used as a fluorescent dye (λ
ex
= 465 nm, λ
em
= 502 nm). A mixture of 50 µL of Cou-6 acetone solution (1 mg/mL) with 1 mL of ART-Ala and AAP acetone solutions (1 mg/mL) was used to prepare Cou-6-encapsulated ART-Ala NPs (Cou 6/ART-Ala NPs) and Cou 6-encapsulated AAP NPs (Cou 6/AAP NPs), following the previous NP preparation method. A total of 1.5 × 10
4
CT26 cells per dish were distributed in 35 mm confocal dishes and incubated for 24 h. The cells were subsequently exposed to Cou6/ART-Ala NPs or Cou6/AAP-Ala NPs for durations of 4, 12, or 24 h. In a competitive assay, the cells were preincubated with 4.0 mM free PBA for 30 min before NP addition. The cells were subsequently fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, washed twice with PBS, and stained with DAPI (Biosharp, Hefei, Anhui, China). The imaging process employed a confocal laser scanning microscope (CLSM; Nikon C2 Plus, Tokyo, Japan). Cellular drug uptake was quantified by flow cytometry (FCM; BD FACSymphony A1, Franklin Lakes, New Jersey, USA). After treatment with the NPs, with or without free PBA, the CT26 and HCT116 cells were digested, collected, and resuspended in 400 µL of PBS, and their uptake was examined via FCM.
Cell apoptosis assessments
CT26 and HCT116 cells (1.8 × 10
5
cells per well) were seeded in 6-well plates and incubated for 24 h. The cells were then exposed to ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, and AAP NPs for 24 h (NPs concentration: 40 µM). After incubation, the cells were stained with Annexin V-FITC/PI Apoptosis Kit (Elabscience, Wuhan, Hubei, China) according to the manufacturer’s protocol, and FCM quantitatively analyzed the apoptotic cells.
Clonogenic assay
The antiproliferative potential of the NPs was investigated via a clonogenic survival assay. CT26 and HCT116 cells were cultured in media containing ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, AAP NPs, or AAP NPs + DFO (NPs concentration: 20 µM; DFO concentration: 100 µM) for 7 days (6-well plates, 400 cells per well). After that, the samples were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, washed twice with PBS, and stained with 0.1% crystal violet. Colony formation was quantified via ImageJ (version 1.8.0).
Transwell migration and invasion assays
Tumor cells (3 × 10
4
cells/well, CT26 and HCT116 cells) were seeded into the upper chambers of Falcon™ cell culture inserts (BD Bioscience, San Jose, Franklin Lakes, New Jersey, USA) equipped with or without a Matrigel-coated polycarbonate membrane in incomplete medium. In contrast, the lower chambers were supplemented with RPMI 1640 or McCoy’s 5 A medium supplemented with 15% FBS to detect tumor cell migration and invasion ability. After incubation with ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, AAP NPs, AAP NPs + DFO (NPs concentration: 20 µM; DFO concentration: 100 µM) or culture medium for 24 h, the permeate cells were stained with 0.1% crystal violet.
Intracellular ROS generation
H2-DCFDA was used to quantify the ROS levels in the CT26 and HCT116 cell lines. First, 1.5 × 10
4
CT26 and HCT116 cells per dish were placed in 14 mm confocal dishes and incubated overnight. The tumor cells were subsequently exposed to ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, AAP NPs, or AAP NPs + DFO for 24 h (NPs concentration: 30 µM; DFO concentration: 100 µM). Afterward, the cells were washed with cold PBS and stained with a DCFH-DA probe (10 µM) for 40 min at 37 °C. Imaging was conducted via CLSM. Quantification of intracellular ROS levels via FCM. CT26 and HCT116 cells were seeded into 6-well plates and allowed to adhere for 24 h. After being incubated with the NPs for 24 h and then exposed to H2-DCFDA (10 µM) for 40 min, the cells were washed twice with cold PBS and analyzed via FCM.
LPO level and MDA content evaluation
The CT26 and HCT116 cell lines were exposed to ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, or AAP NPs (NPs concentration: 30 µM) with or without the addition of 100 µM DFO for 24 h. Then, the CT26 and HCT116 cells were incubated with 15 µM C11-BODIPYTM
581/591
(Invitrogen, Carlsbad, California, USA) for 30 min, collected, washed, and analyzed for LPO levels via FCM. To assess malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, the cells were collected after 24 h of exposure to ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, AAP NPs, or AAP NPs combined with DFO (NPs concentration: 50 µM; DFO concentration: 100 µM). Following the manufacturer’s protocol, the intracellular MDA concentration was quantified via an MDA assay kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). This methodology was similarly employed to evaluate the MDA content in tumor tissue samples.
GSH level evaluation
CT26 and HCT116 cells (3 × 10
5
cells per well) were cultured in 6-well plates and maintained overnight at 37 °C. The cells were exposed to ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, AAP NPs, or AAP NPs + DFO for 24 h (NPs concentration: 25 µM; DFO concentration: 100 µM). After incubation, the cells were washed with PBS, and the GSH levels were quantified. A GSH detection kit (Jiancheng, Nanjing, China) was used, as instructed by the manufacturer. An analogous procedure was employed to assess the GSH levels in the tumor tissue.
Determination of GPX4 activity
GPX4 activity in CT26 and HCT116 cells was measured via a GPX4 assay kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). The cells were exposed to ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, AAP NPs, or AAP NPs + DFO for 24 h (NPs concentration: 40 µM; DFO concentration: 100 µM). Afterward, the samples were lysed and centrifuged (12,000×g, 4 °C), after which the supernatants were collected. In a 96-well plate, 50 µL of the supernatant and 40 µL of the GPX4 assay working solution were mixed, and the absorbance at 340 nm was measured at 1 min intervals for 10 min consecutively. Furthermore, the protein concentration in the supernatant was measured via a BCA protein assay kit (Elabscience, Wuhan, Hubei, China).
Western blotting analysis
After 48 h of treatment with ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, or AAP NPs (NP concentration: 30 µM), the cells were lysed on ice in RIPA buffer (Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, Missouri, USA), and the protein concentration was determined via the BCA method. Subsequently, SDS-PAGE was performed on 20 µg of protein in loading buffer, which was then transferred to PVDF membranes. The membranes were blocked and incubated with primary antibodies. The antibodies utilized in this study, along with their respective dilutions, were as follows: GPX4 (1:1000, Proteintech, Wuhan, Hubei, China), SLC7A11 (1:1000, Immunoway, Beijing, China), and β-tubulin (1:1000, Proteintech, Wuhan, Hubei, China), which served as loading controls. The sections were subsequently incubated with secondary antibodies, specifically goat anti-mouse IgG-HRP or goat anti-rabbit IgG-HRP (Proteintech, Wuhan, Hubei, China). A chemiluminescent substrate was then applied to the membranes, which were visualized via a chemiluminescence imaging system (Tanon-5200Multi, Shanghai, China).
Evaluation of the cellular mitochondrial membrane potential
The mitochondrial membrane potential was assessed via JC-1 dye (GlpBio, Montclair, CA, USA). JC-1 aggregates and monomers were detected at excitation/emission wavelengths of 550/590 nm and 485/535 nm, respectively. Following a 24 h incubation period with ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, AAP NPs, or AAP NPs combined with DFO (NPs concentration: 35 µM; DFO concentration: 100 µM), CT26 and HCT116 cells were stained with fresh JC-1 solution (2 µg/mL) for 30 min and subsequently analyzed via CLSM.
Animals
The Experimental Animal Center at China Medical University approved all the animal experiments (Approval number: CMU20240820). Seven-week-old BALB/c female mice weighing 18 to 20 g were purchased from SPF Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). To develop a CT26 tumor-bearing mouse model, a subcutaneous injection of 100 µL containing 1 × 10
6
CT26 cells was administered into the right dorsal region of each mouse. The tumor dimensions were subsequently measured via a digital caliper. When the mouse tumors reached a predetermined volume, the mice were randomly assigned to various groups for in vivo experimentation.
In vivo biodistribution behavior
DiR (Meilunbio, Dalian, Liaoning, China) was used to load the NPs and investigate in vivo biodistribution. The DiR-encapsulated self-assembled NPs (DiR/ART-Ala NPs and DiR/AAP NPs) were prepared by mixing 50 µL DiR (1 mg/mL in DMSO) and 1 mL AAP or ART-Ala (1 mg/mL in acetone) in an aqueous solution.
When the tumors reached an average size of 300 mm³, the CT26 tumor-bearing mice were randomly split into three experimental groups (
n
= 3): free DiR, DiR/ART-Ala NPs, and DiR/AAP NPs, with each mouse given 35 µg of DiR. The mice were intravenously injected via the tail vein with free DiR, DiR/ART-Ala NPs, or DiR/AAP NPs (100 µL) and anesthetized with isoflurane. In vivo, fluorescence images (λ
ex
= 745 nm, λ
em
= 780 nm) were recorded at the indicated times (4, 8, 12, 24, 36, 48, and 60 h) via an IVIS Spectrum system (LB983 NC100; Berthold Technologies, BadWildbad, Black Forest, Germany). All the mice were sacrificed after 60 h to harvest organs and tumors for ex vivo fluorescence imaging, which was used to investigate the biological distribution of the NPs.
Hemolysis assay
The blood samples were centrifuged at 4 ℃ for 10 min (3000 rpm), and erythrocytes were separated and diluted with PBS. Subsequently, the erythrocytes were incubated with NPs (concentration: 10 µM, 25 µM, 50 µM) at 37 ℃ for 1 h. After that, centrifugation was carried out at 4 ℃ for 10 min (1000 rpm), the absorbance of the supernatants were measured at OD 540 nm and calculate the hemolysis rate using the following formula: HP (%) = (OD
e
-OD
saline
)/(OD
H2O
-OD
saline
) × 100% (OD
e
: experimental group; OD
saline
: saline group; OD
H2O
: Sterile ddH
2
O group). Sterile ddH
2
O was used as a positive control, and saline was used as a negative control.
In vivo antitumor efficacy and toxicity evaluation
For the ART-NPs, ART-Ala NPs, and AAP NPs treatment groups, the model mice were randomly assigned to four groups when the average tumor volume reached 100 mm³: the saline, ART-NPs, ART-Ala NPs, and AAP NPs groups (
n
= 8). Various formulations were administered intravenously to the mice on days 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 at a dosage of 20 mg/kg. For the RSL3 and fluorouracil (5-FU) treatment groups, CT26 tumor-bearing mice were divided into four treatment groups: saline, RSL3 (5 mg/kg), 5-FU (55 mg/kg), and AAP NPs (20 mg/kg) (
n
= 8). The tumor volume and body weight of the mice were monitored daily. The formula for calculating tumor volume was as follows: V (mm³) = length (mm) × width (mm)² × 1/2. The mice in each group were euthanized on the 14th day of treatment. Tumor Growth Inhibition (TGI) was calculated to assess antitumor efficacy using the formula: TGI (%) = [1 - (Δ
Treated
/Δ
Control
)] × 100, where Δ
Treated
and Δ
Control
represent the average tumor volume of the treatment group and the control group at the end of treatment, respectively. Next, immunohistochemistry (IHC) was performed on the tumors via H&E, TUNEL (Abcam, Cambridge Science Park, UK), and Ki67 (Abcam, Cambridge Science Park, UK) staining in ART-NPs, ART-Ala NPs, and AAP NPs treatment groups. Each group selected three biologically independent tumor samples for replicate experiments. Mouse survival was independently assessed over a 60-day period.
The levels of GSH and MDA in tumor tissues were quantified via previously described methods. The protein expression of GPX4 and SLC7A11 in tumors was assessed through IHC, while ROS generation in tumors was measured via an immunofluorescence assay. Histological analysis of the main organs was performed via H&E staining. Blood samples were collected to evaluate hepatorenal function.
Transcriptomic sequencing
HCT116 cells were treated with ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, or AAP NPs (concentration: 40 µM) for 24 h. All treated HCT116 cells and control cells were harvested in triplicate and sent to Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing). Using TRNzol Universal Reagent (IANGEN, Beijing, China), total RNA was extracted from HCT116 cells, followed by RNA sequencing on an Illumina NovaSeq platform by Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). The initial step involved aligning the sequencing reads to the human reference genome (version hg38) via HISAT2 software. The read counts were counted and mapped to each gene using FeatureCounts v1.5.0-p3.
Proteomic sequencing
The cells were collected 72 h after exposure to ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, AAP NPs, or the negative control (NP concentration: 40 µM). Novogene Co., Ltd. performed the deep data-independent acquisition (DIA) quantitative proteomics analysis, a high-resolution mass spectrometry method that provides a comprehensive digital map of the proteome. SDS-PAGE confirmed that the protein purity and concentration of the extracted protein were accurately determined. After trypsin treatment, LC-MS/MS analysis was performed in DIA mode.
Bioinformatic analysis
Differential expression analysis was subsequently performed with the DESeq2 R package (1.20.0), and differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were defined as those with significant quantitative differences between the experimental and control groups (
p
< 0.05, |log2FC| >1 (FC, fold change)). The protein quantification results were statistically analyzed using a t-test. The differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were defined as those with significant quantitative differences between the experimental and control groups (
p
< 0.05, |log2FC| >0.263, corresponding to a FC > 1.2). The application of a distinct fold-change threshold for DEPs, compared to that used for DEGs, accounts for the higher biological variability inherent to proteomic data and aims to capture more subtle, yet biologically important, changes in protein abundance. Integrated proteome and transcriptome analyses were performed via the NovoMagic platform (
https://magic-plus.novogene.com
). We utilized the cluster Profiler R package to assess the statistical enrichment of DEGs in Gene Ontology (GO) functions, a standardized framework that categorizes gene functions into three ontologies: Biological Process (BP), Cellular Component (CC), and Molecular Function (MF).
Statistical analysis
Data analysis was performed via GraphPad Prism 8, and the data are presented as the means ± standard deviations (SDs). The two groups were compared via an unpaired Student’s
t
test; *
p
< 0.05, **
p
< 0.01, ***
p
< 0.001, and ****
p
< 0.0001 were considered statistically significant; n.s. Indicates no significant difference.
Results
Chemical synthesis of ART derivatives and in vitro cytotoxicity evaluation of derivatives
The chemical synthesis routes for the ART derivatives are depicted in Fig.
1
A and Additional file 1: Fig. S1. ART reacts with 20 natural amino acids by adding HATU and TEA to afford the target compounds ART-amine acid (Additional file 1: Fig. S1A). Prior to conducting the cytotoxicity assay, the SA expression levels in cells were analyzed by western blotting. As shown in Additional file 1: Fig. S2, the expression levels of SA in tumor cells (CT26, HCT116, HuH7, SW620, and SW480 cells) were significantly higher than those in normal cells (NIH/3T3 and HIEC6 cells). Among them, CT26 and HCT116 cells exhibited the highest SA expression, followed by SW620, HuH7, and SW480 cells. Therefore, we selected CT26, HCT116, SW620, and HuH7 cells for the preliminary screening of compound activity. The in vitro cytotoxicity of the derivatives was evaluated in tumor cells via the CCK-8 assay, with ART and dihydroartemisinin (DHA) used as controls. As shown in Additional file 1: Table S1, compared with ART, most compounds presented varying levels of cytotoxicity to CT26 cells. Among them, ART-Phe had the most potent effect on CT26, with an IC
50
value of 16.93 µM, which was 3-fold greater than that of ART, followed by ART-Glu (CT26, IC
50
= 18.57 µM) and ART-Ala (CT26, IC
50
= 26.18 µM). Regarding human tumor cells, ART-Ala was more effective in HCT116 and SW620 cells, with IC
50
values of 29.75 µM and 36.70 µM, respectively. ART-Phe and other compounds did not exhibit significantly greater cytotoxic effects on HCT116 and SW620 cells compared to ART. In addition, since COC patients are prone to developing liver metastasis [
42
], we evaluated the cytotoxicity of HuH7 cells. As expected, ART-Ala displayed the optimal cytotoxicity for HuH7, with an IC

Preparation and characterization of ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, and AAP NPs
Drug solubility is closely linked to drug release and in vivo bioavailability. Compared with those of ART, the water solubilities of ART-Ala and AAP were significantly improved by more than 50-fold and 6-fold, respectively (Additional file 1: Fig. S3), indicating that advisable structural modification strategies were employed. However, AAP and AAS had decreased solubilities compared with ART-Ala and ART, respectively, which may be related to the strong hydrophobicity of the benzene ring structure. Therefore, there is a need for advisable strategies to improve solubility further.
Nanotechnology can potentially increase the water solubility of poorly soluble drugs, thereby increasing their bioavailability and biological effectiveness [
43
–
45
]. Given this, the NPs of ART, ART-Ala, and AAP were formulated to enhance water solubility and bioactivity further. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images revealed that the average size of the three nanoparticles is less than 200 nm (Fig.
1
C top). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images confirm their uniform spherical structure, smooth surface, and well-monodisperse nature (Fig.
1
C, bottom). Dynamic light scattering measurements revealed that the ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, and AAP NPs had sizes of 169 nm, 139 nm, and 151 nm, with polydispersity indices (PDIs) of 0.133, 0.132, and 0.045, respectively. In terms of zeta potential, AAP NPs (−28 mV) were similar to ART NPs (−23 mV) and ART-Ala NPs (−25 mV) (Fig.
1
D). Moreover, probably due to the presence of many ions, the sizes of the NPs in PBS and PBS with 10% FBS were slightly larger than those in water. They exhibited minor changes over time, indicating improved physiological stability of the prepared NPs (Additional file 1: Fig. S4). Drug release from the NPs was subsequently conducted at pH levels of 7.4, 6.5, and 5.5. As shown in Fig.
1
E, the amount of drug released from AAP NPs was approximately 25% under typical physiological conditions for 48 h. However, greater drug release (>90%) was observed after AAP NPs were incubated at pH 6.5 and 5.5 for more than 12 h, indicating the stability of AAP NPs under physiological conditions and the acidic dissociation of AAP NPs from tumors. Similar trends were observed for ART NPs and ART-Ala NPs.
Given that PBA can specifically bind to SA overexpressed on tumor cell surfaces, cellular uptake was used to evaluate the targeting potential of the NPs. The CLSM imaging results indicated that the NPs could be effectively internalized by cells and that the NPs were distributed principally in the cytoplasm (green fluorescence) after endocytosis (Fig.
1
F and Additional file 1: Fig. S5). Notably, AAP NP-treated CT26 cells exhibited greater cellular uptake than that of ART-Ala NPs (brighter green fluorescence), with the intracellular fluorescence increasing over time. In addition, free PBA, as a competitive ligand, reduced the fluorescence intensity in the AAP NPs group but not in the ART-Ala NPs group, suggesting active recognition during AAP NPs accumulation. The FCM results revealed that the fluorescence intensities of CT26 and HCT116 cells treated with AAP NPs for 24 h were 1.4- and 1.7-fold greater than those of the ART-Ala NPs group, respectively (Fig.
1
G and Additional file 1: Fig. S6). Furthermore, compared with CT26 cells, HCT116 cells presented a greater mean fluorescence intensity (MFI), suggesting enhanced uptake and a greater likelihood of improved anticancer efficacy in HCT116 cells. These findings suggest that the prepared NPs are conducive to subsequent in vitro and in vivo studies.

In contrast to free drugs (ART, ART-Ala, and AAP), the NPs showed enhanced antiproliferative activities, with AAP NPs being the most effective. The NPs exhibited weak cytotoxicity to NIH/3T3 cells, indicating a potentially safer profile. Potential mechanism of AAP NPs-induced cell death in vitro
To verify the capacity of the NPs to induce ferroptosis, we examined alterations in cell viability following treatment with ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, or AAP NPs in combination with or without the ferroptosis inhibitors DFO and Fer-1 (ferrostatin-1, an antioxidant). As shown in Fig.
3
A, the two ferroptosis inhibitors mitigated the cytotoxicity of AAP NPs. DFO could improve cell survival more effectively than Fer-1, possibly due to the iron-chelating effect of DFO, and reduce the rate of the Fenton reaction, thereby causing a proportion of drug molecules to be uninvolved in the reaction. The presence of DFO promoted only HCT116 cell survival, and Fer-1 prevented death in only CT26 cells in the ART-Ala NPs group. However, the two inhibitors had negligible effects on tumor cells in the ART-NP group, which may be related to the poorer activity of ART NPs at this dose. The above results demonstrate that AAP NPs may induce cell death via a ferroptotic mechanism.
Next, we focused on the capacity of AAP NPs to induce oxidative damage in cells. Since Fe
2+
can break the peroxide bridge bond of ART oxidatively through the Fenton reaction, promoting the formation of oxygen radicals, we evaluated the ROS levels in CT26 and HCT116 cells following treatment with NPs. The CLSM images revealed that the cells in the ART NPs, ART-Ala NPs, and AAP NPs groups presented stronger green fluorescence than those in the PBS group (Fig.
3
B and Additional file 1: Fig. S9A). In contrast, the AAP NPs group presented significant fluorescence enhancement, implying that AAP NPs could stimulate cells to generate more ROS. Moreover, the addition of DFO decreased the fluorescence intensity of the AAP NPs group, suggesting that DFO inhibited ROS production. The FCM analysis also demonstrated that AAP NPs resulted in a concentration-dependent increase in ROS in the two cell lines (MFI, 1.6- and 1.8-fold) relative to the ART NPs group (Fig.
3
C and Additional file 1: Fig. S9B). Moreover, the MFI in the AAP NPs group decreased 1.4- and 2-fold with the addition of DFO.
LPO is a hallmark of ferroptosis, and C11-BODIPY
581/591
was employed to detect the intracellular LPO level. Figure
3
D and Additional file 1: Fig. S10 show that the FITC fluorescence intensities of CT26 and HCT116 cells treated with AAP NPs increased by 20% to 65% compared with those of the ART NPs and ART-Ala NPs, indicating considerable LPO stress, which decreased significantly when AAP NPs were combined with DFO. Furthermore, LPO generation varied with concentration and decreased significantly when AAP NP was combined with DFO. This observation was corroborated by the stable levels of malondialdehyde (MDA), the end product of LPO in stable cell lines (Fig.

GSH is primarily stored in mitochondria and plays a crucial role in cellular defense against oxidants. 3
F). In addition, GSH is a cofactor that is indispensable for the antioxidant activity of GPX4. Its depletion indirectly inhibits GPX4 activity and amplifies oxidative stress. As expected, the NPs had inhibitory effects on the activity of GPX4 in both COC cell lines, with AAP NPs exhibiting the most potent effects, which were reversed by DFO (Additional file 1: Fig. S11). Discussion
The frequent recurrence of COCs leads to the highest number of cancer-related fatalities, and existing standard treatments have not succeeded in enhancing the survival rates of patients with metastatic cancer, highlighting the urgent need to explore new therapeutic options for targeting cancer. Over the past few years, numerous efforts have been made to develop conventional treatment strategies aimed at reducing chemotherapy resistance. Nevertheless, significant hurdles have impeded the effectiveness of current cancer management, and clinical responses have been limited due to unfavorable off-target effects [
49
,
50
].
The successful translation of several NPs formulations into standard clinical practice has not only validated the core principles of nanomedicine but has also paved the way for the development of more sophisticated, next-generation nanomedicine platforms, such as Doxil
®
and polymeric NPs fabricated from poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) [
51
,
52
]. The clinical application of NPs-based drug delivery systems has marked a significant advancement in oncology, offering solutions to long-standing challenges associated with conventional chemotherapeutics, including poor aqueous solubility, non-specific biodistribution, and dose-limiting systemic toxicities. It opens promising paths to address the immunosuppressive TME, improving patient treatment outcomes. In this work, we designed and synthesized a series of ART derivatives modified with amino acids and phenylboronic acids for the induction of ferroptosis in targeted COC treatment. We also constructed a carrier-free, self-assembled nanomedicine (AAP NPs) to improve water solubility further and enhance the bioactivity of the derivatives. Cytotoxicity and in vivo distribution experiments confirmed the achievement of these design objectives, demonstrating the therapeutic advantages of the NPs.
Small-molecule drugs, including erastin, sorafenib, and ART, have been shown to play significant roles in inducing ferroptosis [
53
,
54
]. Nevertheless, their clinical application is strongly restricted by their poor solubility in water and broad distribution within the body, resulting in potentially severe side effects. Our study introduces a breakthrough solution: a carrier-free nanoassembly (AAP NPs) that integrates ART’s ferroptosis-inducing capability with PBA-mediated active targeting. This design achieves three key advances over prior ART nanoformulations: (1) Self-assembly eliminates the need for inert carriers, maximizing bioactive payload and reducing off-target effects; (2) PBA confers precise SA targeting, enhancing tumor accumulation by 1.7-fold versus non-targeted NPs (Fig.
4
D); (3) The unique ART-Ala-PBA structure enables pH-triggered drug release in acidic tumors (>90% at pH 5.5), minimizing premature leakage (Fig.
1
E).
NP-mediated cell death is a multifaceted process that involves various mechanisms, including apoptosis, necrosis, ferroptosis, and immunogenic cell death (ICD). The interaction of NPs with cellular components often leads to the generation of ROS, which play a critical role in inducing oxidative stress and subsequent cell death pathways. For instance, selenium NPs (SeNPs) have been shown to induce ROS-mediated cell death, particularly in cancer cells, by targeting mitochondria and enhancing oxidative stress, while sparing normal cells [
55
]. In GBM models, saRNA-loaded MPDA nanoparticles (Ang-MMsaNPs) were found to upregulate ALOX15, a lipoxygenase that catalyzes the peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs). This leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, characterized by a reduction in membrane potential and abnormal cristae morphology, ultimately culminating in ferroptotic death [
56
]. The insights into the mechanisms of NP-mediated cell death provide a foundation for the development of nanoparticle-based therapies that can selectively target cancer cells while minimizing damage to normal tissues. The continued exploration of these mechanisms will be essential for advancing the efficacy and safety of nanomedicine in cancer therapy.
Notably, deep DIA proteomics uncovered a previously unreported mechanism: AAP NPs significantly suppress RRM1 (Fig.
7
G, H), a regulatory subunit of ribonucleotide reductase. RRM1 knockdown is known to promote ferroptosis by disrupting the p53-p21-GPX4 axis [
48
]. Our data establish RRM1 as a novel target in ferroptosis-driven COC therapy, with AAP NPs achieving synergistic downregulation of both RRM1 and SLC7A11/GPX4 (Fig.
3
G and
6
A, B). Furthermore, RNA-seq revealed that AAP NPs uniquely modulate autophagy (Fig.
8
D), distinguishing them from ART-Ala NPs, which primarily alter amino acid metabolism. This multimodal action simultaneously targeting ferroptosis execution (ROS/LPO), defense (SLC7A11/GPX4), and auxiliary pathways (RRM1/autophagy) explains the superior in vivo efficacy of AAP NPs (73.5% TGI vs. 33.7% for ART-Ala NPs, Fig.
5
B). However, this study did not focus on investigating the regulatory effect of MMR1 inhibition on downstream signaling pathways, and its precise molecular mechanism remains to be further explored.
Real-time monitoring of NPs’ fate in vivo is crucial for optimizing therapeutic regimens, minimizing off-target effects, and managing treatment resistance. The in vivo behavior of nanoparticles is not static but significantly influenced by particle size, surface charge, surface modifications, administration routes, and individual physiological variations. Although in vivo distribution studies demonstrate that AAP NPs can significantly target tumor accumulation, the presence of SA in normal tissues inevitably introduces off-target risks. Therefore, real-time monitoring technologies such as fluorescence imaging, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), and photoacoustic imaging can be employed to track the full-cycle dynamic processes of nanoparticles, bringing AAP NP therapy closer to clinical objectives. Furthermore, hemocompatibility is an essential safety prerequisite for intravenously administered NPs, as interactions with blood components can lead to hemolysis, thrombosis, or complement activation. The results of the blood compatibility assay demonstrated that AAP NPs possess good blood compatibility and no significant hemolysis at therapeutic doses, indicating their potential clinical application value.
Several bottlenecks hinder the transition of nanomedicine from promising preclinical results to widespread clinical application. The heterogeneity of the EPR effect poses a significant challenge. The dense extracellular matrix within the TME impedes the penetration of nanomedicines. NPs cannot penetrate deep tumor tissues, remaining confined to perivascular regions, which severely limits their therapeutic efficacy. Although the AAP NPs have demonstrated efficacy in COC cell lines and CT26 tumor-bearing mice, the fundamental differences between tumors of different species necessitate the conduct of experiments using “patient-derived tumor models” to verify the tumor-suppressive effect of the NPs on human COC.
Furthermore, subcutaneous xenograft models cannot fully replicate the complex characteristics of the TME in clinical COC, including stromal cell interactions, vascular normalization, and immune cell infiltration. Even if the NPs can inhibit tumors in subcutaneous models, they may fail due to the inability to adapt to the complex clinical TME. Therefore, the therapeutic efficacy of the AAP NPs against in situ tumors still needs further exploration.
The evolution of NP design has progressively moved beyond simple encapsulation toward more complex, multifunctional systems that incorporate active targeting ligands and biomimetic coatings to overcome biological barriers and improve therapeutic outcomes. The path to clinical approval remains fraught with challenges, including the need for scalable and reproducible manufacturing processes, rigorous quality control to ensure batch-to-batch consistency, and comprehensive safety evaluations to address potential immunogenicity and long-term toxicity concerns. The scalability and quality control of carrier-free AAP NPs are of great significance for their clinical application. First, ensuring high consistency and reproducibility between batches during large-scale production presents a significant challenge, which may require the adoption of new technologies, such as microfluidics. Second, traditional high-temperature sterilization can destroy the NPs’ structures, so aseptic production processes or filtration sterilization can be adopted. Ultimately, the long-term stability of the formulation is crucial for ensuring its application, and the development of freeze-dried powder injections may be a viable solution. However, the journey from bench to bedside is fraught with challenges, including manufacturing complexities, regulatory demands, and a still-evolving understanding of nano-bio interactions. Addressing these issues will necessitate sustained interdisciplinary collaboration among material scientists, biologists, clinicians, and regulators to fully realize the promise of personalized nanomedicine for a broader range of cancers.
Limitations and challenges in clinical translation
Although this study has confirmed that AAP NPs can effectively inhibit COC by targeting and inducing ferroptosis, their limitations and the severe challenges in clinical translation must be fully recognized and elaborated. Firstly, the general applicability of AAP NPs needs further validation. Current research conclusions are primarily based on animal-derived cell lines and subcutaneous xenograft models. However, subcutaneous xenograft models cannot fully replicate the complex characteristics of the TME in clinical COC. Therefore, the therapeutic effects of the AAP NPs on human-derived and in situ tumors still require further exploration. Secondly, although we observed that AAP NPs suppress RRM1 expression and downregulate SLC7A11 to enhance ferroptosis, there remain unclear aspects in the upstream signaling pathway between RRM1 and SLC7A11, presenting a critical area for future investigation. Thirdly, the complexity of the human metabolic system differs significantly from that of mice. This discrepancy may lead to unexpected toxic side effects in humans despite the excellent safety profile demonstrated by AAP NPs in mouse models. COC is not a homogeneous disease; the individual variations in tumor cell characteristics and TME features directly interfere with the targeting efficiency and antitumor efficacy of NPs. Therefore, a comprehensive assessment of these differences is essential for improving the clinical efficacy of the NPs.
Safety is the primary prerequisite for clinical translation, and off-target effects are precisely one of the leading causes of “therapeutic injury”. Although SA is overexpressed on the surface of COC cells, low levels of SA are also present on the surface of non-cancerous cells (Additional file 1: Fig.S2). AAP NPs achieve COC targeting relying on the PBA-SA interaction, so AAP NPs will inevitably bind to SA on non-cancerous cells, posing a low but inevitable risk of off-target binding. Furthermore, ensuring high batch-to-batch consistency and reproducibility during the preparation of NPs, as well as the sterilization and long-term stable storage, are significant challenges for their clinical application. The ester bonds, amide bonds, and acetal groups in the AAP NPs structure may undergo hydrolysis in vivo, leading to premature drug leakage or degradation into small-molecule fragments. This not only reduces the effective drug concentration in target tissues but also introduces unknown safety risks to the treatment. Therefore, clarifying the clinical pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) properties, exploring the in vivo stability, and thereby optimizing the administration regimen, improving treatment precision, and reducing toxic side effects are indispensable scientific bases for clinical translation. In conclusion, PBA-modified ART presents a promising new strategy for COC treatment; however, its clinical translation remains challenging. Future research efforts should focus on validating the NPs in more clinically relevant models, resolving process-related issues in large-scale production, and systematically evaluating their PK/PD and safety.
Conclusion
Collectively, AAP NP effectively overcome the limitations of ART’s poor water solubility and improve its low antitumor activity. These findings suggest that introducing amino acid and PBA-targeting motifs is a successful strategy to increase ART’s selectivity and effectiveness, and it is worthy of further development as a novel ferroptosis modulator for treating COCs. Moreover, this study elucidates new mechanisms underlying AAP NPs targeting through the integration of RNA sequencing and proteomic analyses. As a novel modulator with active targeting capabilities that robustly triggers ferroptosis, this unique nanomedicine warrants further exploration for the treatment of COC.
